Bureau Veritas soars 6.6% on a rumor of a takeover by US fund Advent, which the group denies

French certification giant Bureau Veritas finished Wednesday, November 25, at the top of the CAC 40, up 6.6% at €31.80, while the index fell 0.75%. The reason: according to Bloomberg, US fund Advent International is considering a takeover bid. The group says it is not in talks with the fund [1][2][3].

On Tuesday evening, November 24, Bloomberg reported that Advent International is working with advisers on a possible bid for Bureau Veritas. The fund could sell off some of the group's businesses if it bought the company [1][6].
According to Bloomberg, the deliberations are at an early stage and may not lead to a deal. Advent did not comment [6].
On Wednesday, the stock hit an intraday record [4], then closed at €31.80, up 6.6%, the biggest gain on the CAC 40, which itself ended at 7,980.57 points (−0.75%) [2].
In a statement, Bureau Veritas said it “is not engaged in discussions” with Advent and that it does not comment on market rumors [3][5].
Before the rumor, the company was worth about $14.76 billion on the stock market, according to LSEG data cited by Investing.com [4].

Bureau Veritas inspects and certifies buildings, factories, products and ships. In the third quarter of 2026, its revenue reached €1.57 billion, with organic growth of 6.2% (excluding acquisitions) [7].

The key takeaway: the denial is narrow. Bureau Veritas says it is not “in discussions” with Advent [3], but Bloomberg never mentioned discussions: it wrote that Advent is studying a bid on its own [1][6]. Investors therefore kept hoping for an offer, and the stock closed sharply higher while the Paris stock market fell [2].

An investment fund like Advent buys companies with its clients' money and a lot of debt, transforms them, then sells them a few years later. Selling off part of the businesses, as Bloomberg mentions [1][6], helps repay part of the debt and lowers the real price paid.

A takeover would also involve the largest shareholder, French investment company Wendel. After a sale in April 2024, Wendel kept about 26% of the capital and 41% of the voting rights [8]. In March 2025, it launched the sale of another 6.7% of the capital at €27.25 per share [9].
This is not Bureau Veritas's first rumor. In January 2025, merger talks with its Swiss rival SGS sent the stock higher, before being abandoned two weeks later [10][11][12].

Bureau Veritas is part of the CAC 40: if you have a PEA, a life insurance policy invested in French stocks or a CAC 40 index fund, you own a little of it. But a rise on a rumor can vanish in one go if no offer comes: buying on a rumor means betting on information that nobody has confirmed.

How it works: why a takeover rumor makes a stock jump

A tender offer (in French, an OPA) is a proposal to buy all of a company's shares at a set price. To convince shareholders to sell, the buyer has to pay more than the market price: that is the “premium.” As soon as a rumor comes out, investors buy the stock to collect this future premium, and the price rises even before any offer. But it only rises partway, because nothing is certain: the market blends the hoped-for price with the risk of failure. On Wednesday, Bureau Veritas hit an intraday record [4] and then closed lower, at €31.80 [2], after its denial [3]. If the offer is confirmed, the stock can rise further; if it fades, the gain can melt away, as in January 2025 when the stock fell as much as 3.8% on the announcement that talks with SGS had ended [12].
Precedents: takeover rumors and battles
January 14-27, 2025

Bloomberg reveals talks between Bureau Veritas and Swiss group SGS to form a combined company worth about $33 billion. Bureau Veritas stock rises as much as 6.2% the next day [10][11]. On January 27, the two groups announce the end of the talks; Bureau Veritas stock loses as much as 3.8% during the session [12].
A rise on a rumor can disappear within two weeks: over the whole period, Bureau Veritas ended almost unchanged [11].
January 13, 2021

Canadian group Alimentation Couche-Tard proposes to buy Carrefour for about €16.2 billion. Carrefour stock closes up 13%, at €17.54 [13]. The next day, Economy Minister Bruno Le Maire says a “courteous but clear and definitive no” in the name of food sovereignty [14], and Couche-Tard gives up a few days later [15].
In France, the state can block a foreign takeover, even a friendly one: the promised premium evaporates.
June-August 2025

Advent reaches an agreement to buy British measuring-instrument maker Spectris, then enters a bidding war with the fund KKR [16]. KKR wins on August 5 with an offer valuing Spectris at £4.2 billion, and Advent withdraws [16][17].
Advent is already hunting in Europe, and when two funds fight over a target, its shareholders are the ones who win.
To help you understand, not advice to buy or sell.

news.2026-11-26-or-sous-3500-dollars.tit: Gold falls below $3,500 an ounce, its lowest since September 2025: US inflation revives bets on a rate hike
news.2026-11-26-or-sous-3500-dollars.sum: On Wednesday, November 25, an ounce of gold fell below $3,500, its lowest level since September 2025, after US inflation figures came in higher than expected. Markets now see a Fed rate hike in December as almost certain. The yellow metal has lost about 37% since its January record [1][2][6].
news.2026-11-26-or-sous-3500-dollars.poi: Spot gold (for immediate delivery) fell 2% to $3,483.59 an ounce [1]; it lost as much as 3% during the session [4]. On New York's Comex futures market, the drop reached 2.4%, and silver fell 4% [12].
Before the release, gold was already trading near its lowest in fifteen months, weighed down by bets on a rate hike [5].

The trigger: the PCE price index, the Fed's preferred measure of inflation, rose to 3.8% year on year in October, from 3.7% the previous month [3][12]. Excluding energy and food, it reached 3.3%, above the expected 3.2% [3].
Markets put the probability of a 0.25-point Fed rate hike at its December meeting at 96.4% [3].
Paradox: the yield on 10-year US government bonds fell about 9 hundredths of a point, to 4.84% [3], which usually supports gold.

The ounce had crossed $5,000 for the first time in January 2026 [7], peaking at $5,589.38 on January 28 [8]. It has given up nearly 37% since then [6]. The firm BCA Research abandoned its four-year bet on rising gold when the price fell below $3,700 [13].
Shares of gold mining companies fell in the wake [1].
news.2026-11-26-or-sous-3500-dollars.why: The key takeaway: gold pays no interest. When the Fed raises rates, a safe investment like a US Treasury bill pays more, and holding gold “costs” more in lost income. Analysts also cite the rise of the dollar [6]: since gold is priced in dollars, it becomes more expensive for buyers paying in euros, yuan or rupees.

The reversal is spectacular. In January, fears about government debt had propelled gold above $5,000 [14]. Since then, US inflation has stayed high, the Fed is preparing to raise rates, and the yellow metal has lost more than a third of its value [6][3]. Even the fall in long-term rates is no longer enough to support it [3].

What comes next depends mainly on the Fed. A hike in December is almost fully priced in [3]: the real question is the next one. If inflation slows, the pressure on gold could ease; if it accelerates further, new rate hikes would weigh on it again.
news.2026-11-26-or-sous-3500-dollars.for: If you bought coins, bars or a gold fund near the January peak, you have lost about a third of your investment [6]. Gold's fall is also a reminder that rates remain high: loans are expensive, but risk-free investments pay more. Gold remains a very volatile investment that can lose a lot in a short time.

news.2026-11-26-or-sous-3500-dollars.dee: How it works: why gold falls when rates rise

A gold bar pays neither interest nor dividends: it only earns money if its price rises. When interest rates go up, other safe investments, such as government bonds or interest-bearing accounts, pay more, and investors sell their gold to move into them. That is what happened in the early 1980s, when Paul Volcker's Fed pushed its rates toward 20% [11]. The dollar also plays a role: gold is paid for in dollars, so a strong dollar makes it more expensive for the rest of the world [6]. On Wednesday, gold fell even as the 10-year yield declined [3]: bets on the Fed's next hike and the dollar weighed the most.
news.2026-11-26-or-sous-3500-dollars.pas: The ounce reaches $850 at the London fixing, driven by double-digit inflation, the hostage crisis in Iran and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan [10]. Paul Volcker's Fed then raises its rates toward 20% in March 1980 [11].
When safe investments pay more than inflation, gold loses its appeal: it then fell for years [11].
Gold plunges $140.30, or 9%, to $1,361 on April 15, its biggest one-day drop in more than 30 years [9]. Over two sessions, it loses more than 12%, unseen since February 1983 [15].
This tumble was seen as the end of an uninterrupted rise since 2001 [9][15].
The day after its record, gold loses more than 8% in a few minutes, from $5,546 to $5,106 an ounce, according to Bloomberg cited by BFM Bourse [16].
A market that rises very fast can drop just as fast: it was the start of the current slide [6].

“Overcapacity”: Washington proposes tariffs on 14 economies, from 15% for Europe to 35% for Vietnam; China and Brussels reject the accusation

On Wednesday, November 25, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer proposed new tariffs against 14 of the 16 economies targeted by an investigation into industrial “overcapacity”: an extra 20% for China, 15% for the European Union, and up to 35% for Vietnam. Mexico and Norway are spared for now [1][2][3].

After an eight-month investigation, the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) concludes that 14 economies have “unreasonable” practices: China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, India, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia, Singapore, Switzerland and Bangladesh [1][4].

China would pay an extra 20%, on top of tariffs of about 25% dating from Donald Trump's first term [1]. According to NBC, this rate could rise to as much as 40% if negotiations between the two countries fail [5].
Vietnam faces up to 35%, the highest rate, and India up to 25% [1][6]. The rates will respect the 15% cap negotiated with the European Union, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan [1].

For Mexico and Norway, the investigation continues, with no timetable [1]. Products already taxed on national security grounds (“Section 232,” steel or aluminum for example) would not be subject to these new tariffs on top [4].
Jamieson Greer does not expect these tariffs to apply “for two or three months” [5]. They are proposals, open to public comment [1].

Beijing says overcapacity “does not really exist” [1]. “Trade wars are not in the interest of either side,” a spokesperson for China's Commerce Ministry said [7]. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called it a “false proposition” [12].

For the European Commission, spokesperson Olof Gill rejects the idea that Europe is a source of overcapacity: it is rather a victim of it. Brussels demands that any measure stay below the 15% cap agreed in 2025 [8].

Beijing has announced no retaliation. The day before, Tuesday, November 24, its Commerce Ministry even extended until January 27, 2027, the suspension of its ban on exporting gallium, germanium and antimony, metals used in chips, to the United States [9][10]. A separate pause on rare earths runs until January 10 [11].

The key takeaway: Washington is rebuilding its tariff wall with a new legal tool. These measures come a few weeks after the Supreme Court struck down the near-global tariffs Trump had imposed under an economic emergency law [2].

“Section 301” is a 1974 trade law that allows tariffs on a country found guilty of unfair practices, after an investigation and hearings [4][8]. “Overcapacity” is when a country produces far more than it consumes, often thanks to government subsidies, and floods foreign markets with cheap products.
For Europe, the issue is the 15% cap: Greer speaks of a “supplement” to existing tariffs, while Brussels wants everything to stay below that cap [2][8].

If European companies pay more to sell in the United States, some French exports, such as wine, luxury goods or machinery, could suffer. For your purchases in France, the direct effect is small, unless Europe decides to retaliate.

Brussels summit: the 27 wrangle over a €1,780 billion seven-year budget; Merz threatens to block everything if four countries refuse to pay for Ukraine

The leaders of the 27 EU countries meet on Thursday, November 26, and Friday, November 27, in Brussels for a special summit on the 2028-2034 European budget. On the table: a compromise of about €1,780 billion and the financing of Ukraine in 2027. No overall agreement is expected this week [1][3][6][7].

European Council President António Costa presented his compromise, the “negotiating box,” on November 21 [2]. It cuts the Commission's initial proposal by 10%, or €204 billion, to about €1,780 billion in current prices, while keeping up to €100 billion for Ukraine [1].
In 2025 prices, that comes to €1,582 billion, or €40 billion more in cuts than the October version from the Irish presidency. Costa also proposes a 3% tax on digital services [8].
According to EUobserver, the text provides less money for farmers and regions [5]. Costa told the 27 that “the time has come to reach an agreement” [4].
In parallel, on November 18 the Commission presented a new loan of up to €45 billion for Ukraine in 2027, financed by joint borrowing on the markets [9].

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz threatens to block the budget unless all 27 take part in this financing [3]. Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia opted out of the €90 billion loan agreed in April [6], and Bulgaria has signaled it will not pay more [3].

As early as November 10, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico denounced a “textbook case of blackmail” and brandished his own veto: Slovakia has “the same right of veto as Germany” [10]. Czech leader Andrej Babiš points out that the budget already provides €100 billion for Ukraine, but only from 2028 [10].
According to Politico Europe, no agreement is expected this week [7]. Diplomats are aiming for the last summit of the year, which opens on December 17 [6].

The key takeaway: Europe must set its spending for seven years, from 2028 to 2034, in the middle of the war in Ukraine. Each country defends its priorities, and Germany, the largest contributor, is using the budget as leverage to make everyone pay for aid to Kyiv [3][10].

The EU's multiannual budget (the “multiannual financial framework”) funds agriculture, poor regions, research and external action. It requires unanimity: a single country can block everything, hence the weight of veto threats, from Berlin as from Bratislava [3][10].

Kyiv's need is urgent: in his letter to Costa, Merz puts Ukraine's financing gap in 2027 at €70 billion [10]. The €100 billion planned in the European budget will only arrive in 2028, hence this separate €45 billion loan [9][10].

France is the largest beneficiary of the Common Agricultural Policy: less money for farmers means a risk to farm incomes and, eventually, to the prices on your plate. And every billion the EU fails to find in new revenue, such as the digital tax, will have to come from national budgets, and therefore from your taxes.

Crisis in the European Parliament: socialists and liberals walk out on the right, which voted with the far right again; Metsola's reelection in doubt

On Wednesday, November 25, the socialists (S&D) and the liberals of Renew suspended their coalition talks with the center-right EPP. The reason: the EPP passed, with the far right, a text relaxing environmental impact assessments. Roberta Metsola's reelection in January is under threat [1][2].

The trigger is the “Omnibus VIII” text, proposed by the European Commission to speed up environmental assessments of projects. The EPP got it adopted with the votes of far-right groups, against the wishes of its usual partners [1][5].
According to Euronews, this is not the first time: the EPP has already voted several times with the far right since the start of the term [1].

The three groups were negotiating a written agreement for the second half of the legislative term, with shared priorities and working rules [2]. All these talks are suspended “until further notice” [2].

Socialists and liberals demand a written commitment from the EPP to stop voting with the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR), the Patriots for Europe (PfE) and Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) [1][2].

The EPP, for its part, wanted its two partners to back a third term for Roberta Metsola as President of the Parliament in January [3][4]. Within Renew, a written agreement is presented as a precondition for that support [4].

According to Politico Europe, cited by a Ukrainian media outlet, the talks had already derailed on Tuesday, when right-wing lawmakers asked at the last minute to reopen European nature protection laws [3].

The key takeaway: the central majority that has run the European Parliament for years, the right, socialists and liberals, is cracking. The EPP is showing it can find another majority on its right, and its partners are responding by blocking any agreement [1][2].

In the European Parliament, no group has a majority on its own. To pass laws, elect its president or approve the Commission, alliances are needed. Until now, the EPP relied mainly on the socialists and liberals. If it allies more often with the far right, the direction of European laws could shift, especially on the environment [1].

The first concrete deadline is the election of the Parliament's president in January. Without the votes of the socialists and liberals, Roberta Metsola would have to seek support elsewhere, including from the far right, which would confirm the shift [3][4].

The “Omnibus VIII” text is one of the “simplification” laws sought by the Commission to ease the rules imposed on businesses. Its supporters see it as a way to build faster, its opponents as a step back for environmental protection [1][5].

Environmental impact assessments decide whether a road, a factory or a warehouse can be built near you, and under what conditions. Lighter rules mean faster projects, but fewer checks on their effects on nature, water or noise.

Minimum wage: the decree is adopted, the Smic rises to €1,502 net from December 1, “crumbs” according to the CGT

The Council of Ministers on Wednesday, November 25, adopted the decree raising the Smic (France's minimum wage) by 1.6% from December 1, a month before the usual January increase. The minimum wage rises from €1,477.93 to €1,501.94 net per month. Over 2026 as a whole, the total increase reaches 5.3% [1][2][3].

Labor Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou presented the decree to the Council of Ministers on November 25 [1][2]. It implements the announcement made by the Prime Minister at the social conference of November 9 [3].
The gross monthly Smic rises from €1,867.02 to €1,897.35, and the gross hourly Smic from €12.31 to €12.51 [4]. In net terms, that is about €24 more per month [6].

According to the ministry, the total Smic increase over 2026 reaches 5.3%, or about €75 net more per month over a year [3]. The December increase will be deducted from the automatic adjustment in January 2027 [3].

Jean-Pierre Farandou speaks of “a nudge, but also a boost” [6]. The nudge is about 0.6 point: the gap between the 1.6% and what the automatic indexation rule requires [6]. The government presents this increase as the second-largest in 20 years [7].

The unions are not convinced. Marylise Léon, head of the CFDT, calls the increase “insufficient,” while the CGT denounces “crumbs” [8]. They also regret that, in some sectors, negotiated minimum wages remain below the Smic [6].

On the employers' side, Amir Reza-Tofighi, president of the organization Les Entrepreneurs, fears that wages just above the Smic will stagnate, while reductions in social contributions on low wages are to be cut by about ten billion euros in 2027 [6]. Some small businesses find the increase “very complicated” to apply [9].

The key takeaway: the government is bringing the Smic increase forward by a month and adding a small bonus, in response to anger over the cost of living. But neither the unions nor the employers are satisfied [3][8][6].

Normally, the Smic rises every January 1 according to an automatic formula that tracks inflation and part of wage growth. The government can add a “coup de pouce” (a nudge), meaning an increase beyond the formula. That is what it is doing here, by about 0.6 point [6].
The timing is not neutral.

The flip side: when the Smic rises faster than other wages, more and more employees end up paid the minimum. That is the concern expressed by employers [6], and an increase that “raises questions” according to legal experts [5].

If you are paid the Smic full time, your December payslip should show about €1,502 net, or €24 more. If you earn a little more, nothing requires your employer to follow suit: it is up to negotiations in your sector or company.

Canada: Governor Tiff Macklem warns it may be necessary to “raise rates”; markets put 80% odds on a hike on December 9

On Tuesday, November 24, in Toronto, Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem warned that the surge in oil prices risked spreading to other prices and that a rate hike could be necessary. Markets now put the probability of a hike on December 9 at 80%, and BMO bank is forecasting one [1][3][5].
Tiff Macklem was speaking before the Economic Club of Canada [1]. He said he expects “second-round inflation” linked to the oil shock: the rise in energy costs would spread to other prices [1].
“If inflation stays too high for too long, we will have to raise rates,” he warned [1].
The central bank's policy rate is 2.5%, after a quarter-point hike in October [2].
In October, the Bank of Canada forecast inflation of 3.5% at year-end. The governor notes, however, that oil and refinery margins have fallen, suggesting that inflation “may not be as high” [4].

He also clarified his compass: “Total inflation is our target.” The indexes that strip out the most volatile prices only serve to forecast where inflation is heading [6]. He acknowledged that the bank had sent mixed messages on this point in the past [6].
After the speech, Canadian bonds fell across all maturities: their yields rise when investors expect higher policy rates [3].
BMO bank now expects a hike as early as the December meeting [5].
The key takeaway: like the US Fed, the Bank of Canada is considering raising rates to curb the inflation imported by the oil crisis, even though the economy is showing signs of weakness [1][3].
The dilemma is real: since the last hike, economic data have mostly come in weaker than expected [3]. Raising rates would further slow an economy already hit by the trade war with the United States.

Before deciding, the bank is waiting for third-quarter growth and November employment figures, released next week [4]. The central bank and Ottawa have also just renewed for five years the monetary policy framework, which sets the inflation target [2].

For you in France, the effect is indirect: a rate hike in Canada would strengthen the Canadian dollar, which would make a trip or studies in Quebec a little more expensive in euros. Above all, it is one more sign that the oil crisis is pushing central banks to raise rates.

news.2026-11-26-mexique-gomez-mont-note-: Mexico: Washington lets a fugitive wanted by Mexico leave for Spain; Sheinbaum sends a protest note and demands “reciprocity”

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum announced on Wednesday, November 25, that she had sent a diplomatic note of protest to the United States, which let former TV host Inés Gómez Mont, the subject of arrest warrants in Mexico, leave for Spain instead of handing her over to Mexico [1][2][3].
Inés Gómez Mont had been held since October 30 in a migrant detention center in Florida [1].
Washington explains that she entered the United States with a Spanish passport, as she has dual nationality; the US Department of Homeland Security speaks of a “voluntary departure” [1].
Sheinbaum also criticizes the withdrawal of Interpol's international wanted notice (“red notice”) and will protest to the organization [1][3].
Mexico has already requested her extradition from Spain [1][4].
The key takeaway: the president points out that Mexico has sent 94 suspects to the United States and demands the same in return [1].
Sheinbaum also cited the Ayotzinapa case, the disappearance of students that haunts the country, among the cases where she expects Washington's cooperation [1].
The fugitive is now in Spain, an EU country: it is the Spanish courts that will decide whether or not to send her back to Mexico.

news.2026-11-26-turquie-haftar-ankara-er: Turkey: Erdogan hosts Libyan Field Marshal Haftar, his former civil war enemy, for the first time

Eastern Libya's military leader, Khalifa Haftar, was received on Wednesday, November 25, in Ankara by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, for his first official visit to Turkey, hailed as a “new phase” in relations [1][2].
Haftar was accompanied by his son Saddam Haftar, presented as his likely heir, according to a photo released by the Turkish presidency [2].
He also met the Turkish foreign and energy ministers, as well as the head of the intelligence services [3].
The Turkish presidency gave no details about the closed-door talks; Haftar's office spoke of “the latest regional and international developments” [2][3].
According to Turkish diplomats, he arrived on Tuesday at Erdogan's invitation [3].

The key takeaway: during the Libyan civil war, Turkey backed the UN-recognized government in Tripoli against Haftar's forces. Hosting its former adversary shows that Ankara now wants to talk to all sides [1][2].

Libya remains divided between the west, governed from Tripoli, and the east, held by Haftar. By talking to both sides, and bringing its energy minister to the table, Ankara is positioning itself to influence the country's future [2][3].
Libya is a major departure point for migrants heading to Europe and an oil supplier: who holds influence there also matters for France.

news.2026-11-26-banque-de-coree-taux-3-2: South Korea: the central bank raises its rate to 3.25%, the highest in two years, buoyed by the chip boom

On Thursday, November 26, the Bank of Korea raised its policy rate by a quarter point, from 3% to 3.25%, the highest in two years. It is its third hike since July, in the face of stronger-than-expected growth and stubborn inflation [1][2][3].
Inflation slowed from 3.1% year on year in August to 2.8% in October, but remains well above the 2% target [2][4].
Growth is surprising: +1% in the third quarter, compared with 0.3% forecast in August. The forecast for 2027 rises from 2.9% to 4.1% [2][3].
The decision was not unanimous: two of the committee's seven members wanted to keep the rate unchanged [2].
On the Seoul stock exchange, the Kospi gained 1.88% after the announcement [3].

The key takeaway: the policy rate is the price at which the central bank lends to banks. By raising it, the bank makes credit more expensive to cool prices, while chip exports are running the economy at full throttle [1][3].

The won also matters: according to a Bank of Korea analysis cited by SBS, a widening rate gap with the United States pushes the won down [4]. For Gareth Leather (Capital Economics), the hiking cycle is nearing its end [3].
If the hike supports the won, Korean products sold in Europe (phones, cars) may cost a little more. And the fight against inflation is not over, in Asia as in the United States.
